artworks.title: The Birth of Athena (Attic black-figure neck-amphora, attributed to the Antimenes Painter)
artworks.description: On this late-archaic Attic neck-amphora from Vulci, now in the British Museum (1836,0224.10), Athena springs fully armed from the head of the enthroned Zeus while the divine company looks on. The museum reading of the scene names Eileithyia twice over: the goddess of birth stands at each side of the emerging Athena, framing the miraculous labor between Hermes and Hephaistos. It is the canonical iconography of the doubled Eileithyiai as midwives, their presence marking the threshold moment when a new divinity first comes to the light.

artworks.title: The Birth of Athena (Attic black-figure amphora, Louvre F32)
artworks.description: On this black-figure amphora in the Louvre (F32), Athena is born from the forehead of Zeus, who had swallowed her mother Metis. As the goddess emerges, Zeus reaches out and grasps the clothing of the attendant goddess of birth at his right, the gesture of a labor steadied by a divine midwife. The scene belongs to the same sixth-century tradition that placed Eileithyia at Athena's delivery, the helper-figure whose outstretched hand eases even an immortal birth into being.

artworks.title: Eileithyia Assisting at the Birth of the Infant Dionysos (engraving after an antique relief)
artworks.description: This engraving in the print collection of the Statens Museum for Kunst (KAS320), reproducing an antique relief composition, is titled in the museum catalogue 'Eileithyia helping at the birth of the child Dionysos, with Hermes standing at left.' The goddess of childbirth bends to the newborn god while Hermes waits to carry the infant away, an intimate threshold scene between deliverance and rescue. It shows Eileithyia in her core role beyond the Olympian births: the bringer of light who attends each delivery and hands the new life onward.
